For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

content.text:
As stated, this asks for a determination that is **not presently known**. In particular, the general implication defining \(S\) is an open Oka-complement problem.

The established complement theorem is that
\[
K\subset\mathbb C^n\ \text{compact and polynomially convex},\quad n\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\ \text{is Oka}.
\]
One cannot replace “polynomially convex” here by “the closure of a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain” as an established general theorem. Smooth pseudoconvexity does not imply polynomial convexity; it does not even guarantee a Stein neighbourhood basis. Thus this theorem does not determine \(S\) in the question.

There is a useful necessary implication in dimension two:
\[
2\in N.
\]
Indeed, if \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\), its Levi form is negative at some boundary point. With the orientation reversed, the complement has a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point. A local peak function there, truncated and extended by a constant, gives a nonconstant bounded plurisubharmonic function on the complement. An Oka manifold cannot admit such a function: convex approximation implies strong dominability, and bounded-above plurisubharmonic functions pulled back to \(\mathbb C^m\) are constant.

Consequently, the requested exact pair cannot currently be supplied without resolving an open problem:
\[
\boxed{\text{The exact ordered pair }(S,N)\text{ is not presently known.}}
\]

The team did **not** prove \((S,N)=(\mathbb Z_{\ge2},\varnothing)\). Instead, they established directly from the problem’s approximation definition that

Thus the prescribed conclusion \(N=\varnothing\) is false. Their argument does not determine the full pair \((S,N)\), and they proved no general forward implication establishing membership in \(S\).

## Complete argument establishing \(2\in N\)

The proof has two elementary analytic ingredients.

### 1. The stated Oka property forces bounded continuous plurisubharmonic functions to be locally constant

Let \(Y\) satisfy the problem’s Oka approximation property, and let \(u:Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, plurisubharmonic, and bounded above.

Take any sufficiently small affine disc
\[
f(\zeta)=p+\zeta v
\]
whose image on a neighbourhood of \(\overline{\mathbb D}\) lies in \(Y\). Applying the definition with \(m=1\) and \(Q=\overline{\mathbb D}\), obtain entire maps \(F_j:\mathbb C\to Y\) converging uniformly to \(f\) on \(\overline{\mathbb D}\).

Each \(u\circ F_j\) is a bounded-above subharmonic function on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant by subharmonic Liouville. Continuity of \(u\) gives, for every \(\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb D}\),
\[
u(f(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(0))
=u(f(0)).
\]
Therefore \(u\) is constant on every sufficiently small affine disc, and so locally constant on \(Y\). No connectedness assumption on the whole exterior is needed.

### 2. A strictly pseudoconvex boundary point produces a forbidden bounded psh function

Suppose \(Y\) has a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point \(q\). Choose a local defining function \(r\) with \(Y=\{r<0\}\) near \(q\), and translate \(q\) to \(0\).

Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(\ker\partial r(0)\) implies that, for sufficiently large \(A>0\),
\[
R=r+Ar^2
\]
has positive-definite full complex Hessian at \(0\). Indeed,
\[
R_{j\bar k}(0)=r_{j\bar k}(0)+2A\,r_j(0)r_{\bar k}(0),
\]
so the added term supplies positivity in the complex normal direction. After shrinking the neighbourhood, \(R\) and \(r\) have the same sign.

The quadratic Taylor expansion can be written
\[
R(z)=2\operatorname{Re}h(z)+H(z)+o(\|z\|^2),
\]
where \(h\) is holomorphic quadratic with \(h(0)=0\), and \(H\) is positive definite. Consequently, for some \(c,\delta>0\),
\[
\operatorname{Re}h(z)\le -c\|z\|^2
\quad\text{on }\overline Y\cap B_\delta.
\]

Choose \(0<\eta<c\delta^2\). Define on \(Y\)
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\operatorname{Re}h(z),-\eta\},&z\in B_\delta,\\
-\eta,&z\notin B_\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
The strict inequality on the artificial sphere gives a collar where the inside formula equals \(-\eta\), so the gluing is valid. The resulting function is bounded, continuous, and plurisubharmonic. Along an interior normal approaching \(q\), it tends to \(0\), while its interior values near \(q\) are negative. Hence it is not locally constant.

This contradicts ingredient 1. Thus an Oka domain, with the definition in the question, cannot have a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point.

### Application in dimension two

If \(\partial K\) is not pseudoconvex in \(\mathbb C^2\), its Levi form is negative in some nonzero complex-tangential direction at some point. The complex tangent space there is one-dimensional, so the exterior defining function \(r=-\rho\) has strictly positive tangential Levi form: the exterior has a strictly pseudoconvex boundary point.

Therefore
\[
\mathbb C^2\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex},
\]
proving \(2\in N\).

Agent 3 also supplied a stronger local obstruction: for the function above, \(W=\{u>-\eta\}\) is nonempty and bounded. Any entire curve meeting \(W\) has constant \(u\)-composition, stays in \(W\), and is therefore itself constant by coordinatewise Liouville. A nonconstant affine disc in \(W\) cannot satisfy the required entire approximation property.
